# The Country of Night

When I was nine, a summer storm knocked the power out for one whole evening. I remember the strangeness more than the fear: the refrigerator sighing into silence, the digital clocks blinking blank, the house suddenly holding its breath. My parents found candle stubs and a flashlight whose cone seemed feeble, almost apologetic, against so much dark. And then someone—my mother, I think—said the thing nobody says anymore: *let's go outside.*

We stood in the driveway while the storm moved off eastward, taking its lightning with it. Above us the clouds tore open, and there it was: the Milky Way, arched from one horizon to the other like a river glimpsed from the air. My father pointed at it without naming it, because what was there to name? The neighbor kids drifted out of their houses one by one, and everyone spoke more quietly than usual, without anyone instructing them to. Darkness enforces its own etiquette.

Near midnight the power snapped back on. The porch light bloomed, the yard went flat and orange, and the sky closed like a book. I didn't know then that the darkness had been lent to us, not given—that across my lifetime it would gradually be recalled. I know now. And I have spent a good deal of time since thinking about what exactly we gave away when we traded the night for the light, and whether the trade was as obviously good as it seemed.

## The Sovereign Night

For nearly all of human history, night was a sovereign power. When the sun went down, the world reorganized itself completely. Travel stopped. Work stopped. The fire became the center of gravity, and around it the day's second life began: food, talk, stories, sleep. But—and this is the part we've forgotten—the world outside the firelight remained perfectly legible. The moon was a calendar and a lamp, waxing and waning on schedule. The stars wheeled overhead with the reliability of clockwork. Every shepherd, sailor, farmer, and child was a working astronomer, fluent in a sky that served as map, almanac, and scripture all at once.

Historians have uncovered something even stranger about how our ancestors inhabited those hours. Roger Ekirch, digging through diaries, court records, and medical texts from the centuries before electric light, kept running into references to "first sleep" and "second sleep"—in French *premier sommeil*, in Italian *primo sonno*. People didn't sleep through the night. They slept hard for a few hours, woke naturally around midnight, and then stayed up for a while—a quiet interval they used for prayer, reflection, conversation, tending the fire, intimacy, sometimes visiting neighbors, occasionally committing small crimes. Only then did they lie back down for the morning sleep. Laboratory studies later confirmed the pattern: when modern volunteers are given fourteen hours of darkness and nothing else to do, they drift into exactly this biphasic rhythm, with a calm, dreamy watch in the middle of the night that many described as the most peaceful state they'd ever been in.

Which suggests that the deep night was never dead time to be skipped over. It was a furnished room in the house of the day. Sleep was not a wall but a tide, and the exposed flats between the waves belonged to the mind. Night was peopled, too—with spirits, ancestors, saints, wandering souls—precisely because ordinary sight failed there. Imagination had jurisdiction over whatever light couldn't reach. Fear and wonder kept the same address.

## Reading by Shadow

And cultures didn't merely endure all that darkness; they *read* it. Some Aboriginal Australian traditions trace the figure of the Emu in the Sky not along the stars but along the Coalsack, the great dark nebula beside the Southern Cross—a constellation made entirely of shadow. Andean astronomers mapped dark-cloud constellations of their own: a celestial llama, a fox, a toad, silhouetted against the glowing river of the Milky Way. To them, the darkness itself carried pattern, character, meaning. The black patches were not holes in the picture. They were the picture.

The night sky was infrastructure, too—shared, free, and astonishingly precise. Polynesian wayfinders crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific holding star paths in their memories, each island approached by steering toward a star that rose or set above it. The heliacal rising of the Pleiades marked the new year in half the world's calendars. Planting, harvest, flooding, migration—all keyed to risings and settings that any attentive person could verify with their own eyes. Every generation handed down the sky the way we hand down passwords now, except the sky required no subscription and belonged to everyone equally.

## Annexing the Dark

The counterrevolution began, as revolutions do, with money. Artificial light was always expensive: tallow candles smoked, beeswax cost a fortune, and the finest illumination of all came from whale oil—spermaceti burned bright and clean, and American whaling fleets chased it across every ocean on Earth. Whole coastal towns were built on the business of lighting other people's evenings. Then came gas: London's Pall Mall glowed under it in 1807, city centers stopped going fully dark, and Paris burnished its claim as the City of Light.

But the true conquest arrived with Edison. His Menlo Park demonstrations on New Year's Eve, 1879, drew crowds who watched incandescent bulbs burn with the awe usually reserved for miracles, and in 1882 his Pearl Street station began sending current to a handful of Wall Street offices—the first customers of a grid that would eventually swallow the planet. What followed was a century of annexation. Streetlights, neon, headlights, floodlights, the refrigerator humming faithfully at three in the morning, the office tower lit for no one. We didn't just illuminate the night; we redrew its borders, extended the day indefinitely, and turned darkness into a resource to be mined like coal. The night became something we extract value from rather than something we inhabit.

## The Unrecognizable Sky

The bill for all this is written in the sky. The 2016 world atlas of artificial night sky brightness found that a third of humanity—including roughly eighty percent of North Americans—can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Worse, it's accelerating: citizen scientists measuring the brightness of the sky overhead have suggested it may be brightening by around ten percent a year, which means it doubles in less than a decade. Most children being born tonight will, in all likelihood, never see the galaxy that contains their home from anywhere near their home.

There's an anecdote that captures the depth of this forgetting better than any statistic. When the 1994 Northridge earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles, worried residents called local observatories to report a vast, strange, silvery cloud hanging in the sky—some suspected the quake itself had caused it. It was the Milky Way. The sky had come back after decades of absence, and people no longer recognized it. They assumed it was an anomaly, an omen, possibly a threat. That is what we have done: not merely lost the stars, but made them foreign. You cannot mourn what you cannot identify.

## The Biological Ledger

Our bodies, meanwhile, kept the old schedule. In darkness, the pineal gland releases melatonin, the hormone that orchestrates sleep, immune function, and repair. Light suppresses it—and blue-rich light, exactly the spectrum our LEDs emit most cheaply and abundantly, suppresses it most efficiently of all. Night-shift workers live at war with this machinery; international cancer researchers classify shift work as a probable carcinogen. The ledger of disrupted circadian rhythms—sleep debt, metabolic trouble, low mood—is long, and most of us carry entries in it without knowing.

Wildlife pays more directly. Sea turtle hatchlings instinctively scramble toward the brighter horizon, which for millions of years meant the moonlit sea; a beachfront glowing with electric light sends generations of them marching inland, to die on the highway or in a pool drain. Migrating birds navigate by stars and by senses we barely understand, and brightly lit buildings and towers kill staggering numbers of them each season. After the attacks of September 11th, researchers studying the Tribute in Light memorial found tens of thousands of birds circling helplessly in the beams; when the lights were briefly extinguished in intervals, the birds dispersed at once. Even the insects are implicated in ways we're only beginning to see—new high-speed footage suggests that moths spiral into our bulbs because they tilt their backs toward the light as though it were the open sky, an ancient orientation reflex cruelly hijacked. Fireflies, who speak to each other in flashes, are trying to hold conversations in a stadium during halftime. Each fixture is trivially small. Their sum is a quieter kind of extinction—not of species, at least not yet, but of habitat: the loss of night itself as a place where life can happen.

## Forty Minutes to See

Here is what redeems all of it: the eye still remembers the way. Human vision is built for this country. Walk out into genuine darkness and your retinas begin a slow chemical renovation—rhodopsin regenerating in the rod cells—and over thirty or forty minutes your sensitivity improves by a factor of a hundred thousand. Your peripheral vision, densest with rods, turns out to see fainter things than the center of your gaze, which is why seasoned stargazers look slightly askance at the objects they want to see. Darkness rewards patience like almost nothing else in modern life.

And the reward, on a clear night far from town, is absurd: the Andromeda galaxy, a vast island of several hundred billion stars, two and a half million light-years away, visible to the naked eye as a faint luminous smear. Think about what that means. Without any instrument, using meat and chemistry alone, you are receiving light that left before our species existed. For most of us, it is the most distant thing we will ever see with our own eyes—and it is available, free of charge, to anyone willing to stand in the dark for forty minutes. Darkness, entered properly, is not blindness. It is the widest aperture we will ever possess.

## Where Everything Begins

It's worth noticing, too, that darkness is not empty. It is where things begin. Seeds germinate underground in complete blackness; roots spend their whole lives exploring it. Gestation happens behind walls of flesh. Ideas famously arrive in showers and on thresholds, in the loose hypnagogic state between sleeping and waking—which makes me wonder whether the old segmented night, with its tranquil middle watch, wasn't an entire institution of reflection that we dismantled without ever reading its charter.

Scale the thought upward. The painters of Chauvet worked thirty-some thousand years ago in chambers no ray of sunlight ever reached, by the flicker of stone lamps burning animal fat—the first art in the world was made in absolute darkness, by choice. Scale it further. After the Big Bang came a cosmic dark age lasting hundreds of millions of years before the first stars ignited; and even now, everything that shines—every star, every galaxy, every candle—is a thin frosting on a universe that is overwhelmingly composed of what we call, tellingly, *dark* matter and *dark* energy, some ninety-five percent of everything, still essentially unexplained. Darkness is not the exception in the cosmos. It is the rule. We live our entire lives in the exception, and have somehow convinced ourselves the exception is the whole.

## Switching It Off

The good news is almost embarrassing: light pollution is the rare pollutant with no half-life, no cleanup, no legacy. Switch it off and it vanishes, instantly and completely. The fixes are mundane—fixtures that aim downward instead of splashing sideways into the sky, warmer bulbs, dimmers, timers, cities going dark during migration season. One Chicago study found that simply dousing the window lights of a single convention center cut bird collisions by more than half. Around the world, more than two hundred certified dark-sky places now guard remaining darkness the way we guard watersheds—as public property, worth defending.

And personally, the remedy is older than any policy: go find it. Drive past the last orange halo of the suburbs. Give your eyes their honest forty minutes. Watch the Milky Way condense out of apparent nothing, the way breath appears on glass—slowly, then all at once, until you're standing inside the river my father pointed at from a blackout driveway decades ago.

That night ended when the power came back, and for a long time I thought of the darkness as the interruption and the light as the normal thing. I have it backward now. Light is the event; darkness is the condition—the page beneath the ink, the silence the music stands in, the country every lamp is only temporarily stationed in. The oldest country is still right there, patient as anything that predates us. It doesn't need to be built or bought or defended with anything more complicated than a switch.

Turn off the porch light sometime. The border is closer than you think, and the whole territory comes back the moment you stop occupying it.
